Languid means slow, weak, and lacking energy or enthusiasm — but in a relaxed, dreamy way rather than a sick or broken-down way. It is the feeling of having no desire to move, rush, or exert yourself, often because of heat, tiredness, or a deep sense of calm.

Think of lying in a hammock on a hot summer afternoon. Your limbs feel heavy. You are not sick. You are not sad. You simply have zero motivation to get up and do anything. Every movement you make is slow and effortless, almost like you're moving through warm water. That state — that soft, slow, heavy-lidded looseness — is what languid describes.

The word always carries a sense of slowness paired with a kind of pleasant or at least peaceful surrender. A languid person is not rushing anywhere. A languid gesture is one made slowly, without urgency. A languid afternoon is one that stretches out quietly, with nothing happening fast.

Here are some natural examples of how it is used in sentences:

She gave a languid wave of her hand, barely lifting her wrist off the armrest.

The children lay in languid heaps on the grass after hours of playing in the sun.

He spoke in a languid voice, as though even the act of forming words required more effort than he wanted to give.

The river moved in a languid current, barely disturbing the lily pads on its surface.

Notice how in every case, something is moving or happening — but slowly, loosely, without force or energy behind it.

One important thing to understand is that languid can carry either a slightly negative or a slightly positive feeling depending on the context. When used negatively, it suggests someone is being too slow, too passive, or too lacking in drive — someone who is languid when they should be energetic can seem lazy or indifferent. When used positively, or at least neutrally, it suggests a kind of beautiful, unhurried ease — the languid grace of a dancer, or the languid warmth of a slow summer day. Writers especially love this word for its poetic, sensory quality.

Words that are close in meaning to languid include listless, lethargic, sluggish, and leisurely. But there are important differences. Listless suggests a sad or disinterested emptiness — someone listless has lost interest or motivation because of low spirits. Lethargic leans more medical or physical, suggesting a heavy, almost abnormal slowness, often from illness or a health condition. Sluggish is more neutral and mechanical — traffic can be sluggish; a machine can be sluggish. Leisurely simply means unhurried but without any weight or weakness implied at all. Languid, by contrast, always implies a soft physical heaviness, an almost bodily surrender to slowness. It has a sensory, almost atmospheric quality the others lack. It feels like warmth and stillness.

The opposites of languid include energetic, vigorous, brisk, lively, and spirited. Where someone languid drifts through the afternoon, someone energetic attacks it.

A few more things worth knowing about how it behaves as a word. It typically describes people, movements, gestures, voices, smiles, eyes, and atmospheres or settings. You would not use it to describe hard, fast, or mechanical things — a languid car engine or a languid thunderstorm would feel wrong because those things have no sense of bodily ease to surrender. But a languid river, a languid summer afternoon, a languid glance — all of these work beautifully because they carry that same sense of slow, unrushed softness.

One last nuance: languid often appears in writing to set a mood. When an author calls a scene or a character languid, they are usually asking you to slow down, feel the warmth, and sense that nothing urgent is happening. It is a word that almost makes you exhale.

In short — if you ever feel heavy, slow, peaceful, and completely unbothered about rushing anywhere, the word for that feeling is languid.
